A child may be confused by the number of branches of Sanatana Dharma and wonder if it concerns only a few communities. Practices may differ; philosophies may diverge but dharma (principles of living) is common for everyone in society. In fact, Sanatana Dharma is for entire humanity, said Tirukkudanthai Dr. Venkatesh, speaking at the Dharma Rakshana Mahotsava, commemorating the Dasamanotsavam (tenth year of Sri Vidyasheera Tirtha Swamiji heading the Sri Vyasaraja Math), in the presence of Sri Sankara Vijayendra Saraswati of Kanchi Kamakoti Peetam and Sri Ranganatha Yateendra Mahadesikan, the 46th Azhagiyasingar of Sri Ahobila Math.
The various entities of Hinduism fall under the umbrella of the Veda sastras. Spiritual literature such as Bhagavatam, Brahma Sutras, speak of the same thing. The spiritual interpretation or unbroken chain of teachings across generations might differ from one school of thought to the other, but Sanatana Dharma refers to a code of conduct that remains unchanged.
Sanatana means something that is eternal, one with neither a beginning nor an end. Achaloyam Sanatanam , says Lord Krishna, referring to the individual soul. Dharma stands for the set of (moral) rules that every human being should follow. The essential characteristics for a perfect human being include guidelines such as leading a truthful life, following virtuous principles in daily life, respecting one’s guru, kindness to all living creatures, helping everyone, obeying one’s father, among others. In the Ramayana, Rama says, “I will obey my father’s words. This is Sanatana Dharma ,” underscoring the fact that obeying elders is a part of Sanatana Dharma .
Unity is another bedrock of Sanatana Dharma and the efficacy of this is highlighted through the parable of the dove and the hunter. In a forest, a dove kept aloof from its brood. One day, a hunter cast a net over it and only when it was trapped did it realise its folly and asked other doves for help. A horde of doves flew in, held the net in their collective claws and flew away, saving the trapped bird from the hunter.
These principles of Sanatana Dharma are for all and not for a linguistic minority. Like a tree having many branches from a single root, Sanatana Dharma has its roots in the Vedas.
